findings.body: The two-list dedup loop reinvents what the standard library does in one expression. `dict.fromkeys` preserves first-seen order and deduplicates in O(N), while `label in seen` is a linear scan making the helper O(N²) as rows grow.

findings.body: The inner loops compute the same count for every carrier (the carrier variable is never used inside the loop), so the returned mapping assigns an identical value to each carrier. The docstring says it counts combinations "per carrier", but the result is carrier-independent.

findings.body: The `carrier` value is never referenced inside the loop body: `count` depends only on `zones` and `weights`, so the identical nested loops are re-run once per carrier with identical results. findings.title: Compute the count once instead of per carrier

findings.body: The docstring states records arrive in chronological order and promises constant time, yet the body sorts the whole list, which is O(N log N) and contradicts the stated guarantee. If the assumption holds, take the last record directly; if it doesn't, the docstring is wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: For a large queue, an O(N log N) sort runs on every call despite the stated chronological-order guarantee, doing far more work than reading the final element.
findings.title: Drop the sort in newest_queue_id — the docstring already guarantees order

findings.body: cap_manifest's per-tier consumption chunk changes from 76 to 27 under a commit that only claims a refactor. The chunk size determines how much of the value is charged at each tier's rate before moving on, so the returned total for a given input changes.

findings.body: The inner zone/weight double loop does not read `carrier` at all, so it computes the identical count for every carrier. Hoist it out and build the result with `dict.fromkeys`, deleting the three nested loops.
findings.failure_scenario: With C carriers, the same Z×W inner iteration runs C times, so runtime is C× larger than the single pass the result actually requires.

    return dict.fromkeys(carriers, count)
findings.title: Compute the carrier count once instead of per carrier

findings.body: The stated intent is a refactor of 8 pipeline modules, but this hunk replaces a pure allocation helper with a new function that builds a SQL query by interpolating `owner_id` directly into the string. This is a security-relevant addition unrelated to a refactor and introduces a classic SQL injection vector: any caller passing unsanitized input lets an attacker alter the query (e.g. `owner_id = "' OR '1'='1"`).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user-controlled owner_id containing a quote; the crafted value is embedded verbatim in the SELECT, allowing arbitrary rows to be read or the query to be rewritten.
findings.suggestion:
def load_order_rows(owner_id: str, cursor: object) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    """Load queued order rows for one owner through an open cursor."""
    query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
    return [dict(row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
findings.title: Out-of-scope: SQL injection via string-interpolated query

findings.body: The query is built with an f-string, so owner_id is embedded verbatim into the statement. Any caller passing untrusted input (an HTTP id, a message payload) can break out of the quotes and alter the statement — e.g. `' OR '1'='1` returns every customer's orders, and stacked/union payloads can read or modify other tables. cursor.execute accepts bound parameters for exactly this reason.

    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))

findings.body: The new stamp_manifest_checkpoint uses datetime.datetime.utcnow(), which has been deprecated since Python 3.12 and emits DeprecationWarning. findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: owner_id is interpolated straight into the SQL text with an f-string, so any value reaching load_order_rows is executed as SQL rather than as a bound literal. cursor.execute is then called with a single argument, giving the driver nothing to escape. The concrete fix is to pass the query with a placeholder and bind owner_id as a parameter (placeholder style depends on the driver: %s for psycopg2/psycopg, ? for sqlite3); also consider the row-dict conversion below, which is unaffected.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who controls the owner identifier passed to load_order_rows supplies a value such as ' OR '1'='1' -- or a UNION/stacked statement; the payload becomes part of the executed query, letting them read, modify, or exfiltrate arbitrary rows from the orders table (and beyond, depending on DB privileges).
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: Parameterize the owner_id filter to prevent SQL injection

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: events defaults to a list literal, which Python evaluates once at function definition time and reuses for every call that omits the argument. findings.body: This diff rewrites dozens of behavioral constants — notes-length limits, minimum quantities, top-N bucket sizes, merge caps, pricing bracket sizes, fallback thresholds, and fallback rates — across every module, but contains no test changes and no rationale. The pricing helpers likewise move fallback epsilon (0.01/0.05/0.1) and fallback rate (0.25/0.4/0.5) in opposite directions in functions with identical structure.
